intro: CARE is looking to understand what current practices are or are not in place. We researched community policing practices from across the country and gathered this list. It is our understanding that many of these practices are already used by the Stratford Police Department, so this is simply an effort to understand what is currently in place.
definition: Community policing is a department-wide way of working in which officers use long-term partnerships with residents, businesses, and local organizations, plus structured problem-solving, to proactively reduce specific crime, disorder, and fear conditions in identified places. These practices are managed and resourced by the department and all officers are evaluated on that work.

items.title: Beat ownership with problem briefs
items.desc: Each officer has a defined, small beat and maintains a living "problem list" of three priority recurring problems. Once per month, the officer documents SARA steps (Scanning, Analysis, Response, Assessment) for one specific problem, such as chronic disturbances at a location, a nuisance property, or an unsafe crosswalk.

items.title: Built-in community contact quota
items.desc: Officers are required to complete a set number of non-enforcement contacts per shift (e.g., three meaningful conversations with residents, shop owners, or youth workers), logged in CAD/RMS as "community contacts." Supervisors review these for substance during weekly check-ins, the same way they review arrest reports.

items.title: Foot or bike time carved out of each shift
items.desc: Every day tour includes a 30 to 60 minute foot or bike patrol block in a designated micro-hotspot or community location, not as a special detail, but as a scheduled part of the shift. Officers visit the same places routinely (school dismissal, senior housing entrance) to build familiarity and feedback loops.

items.title: Shift-start community intel huddles
items.desc: Roll call includes a 5-minute review of one community-identified problem and the current response plan. Officers are assigned micro-tasks for their shift: check on lighting, speak with a building manager, follow up with a complainant.

items.title: Problem-solving as a standard call outcome
items.desc: For recurring calls at the same address, officers must add a brief problem-solving note and at least one non-traditional option, such as a mediation referral, landlord contact, or mental health liaison, before clearing the incident in the RMS.

items.title: Community meetings during normal duty hours
items.desc: Patrol officers rotate attending existing community meetings (neighborhood associations, PTA, tenant groups) during their shift as one of their assigned tasks, not as extra or overtime duty.

items.title: Victim and complainant feedback as a formal case step
items.desc: For qualifying cases (robberies, burglaries, shootings), detectives schedule at least one non-investigative follow-up conversation about safety concerns and needed environmental changes, such as lighting, cameras, and access control. That feedback feeds into a short "problem memo" shared with patrol or the problem-solving team.

items.title: Repeat location / repeat offender problem packages
items.desc: When detectives identify patterns (same apartment complex, same block, same network of individuals), they build a short problem package: location, pattern, and suggested responses involving community partners such as landlords, outreach workers, schools, and code enforcement. Patrol is then tasked to implement pieces as part of normal duty.

items.title: Case closure with a community brief-back
items.desc: For high-impact cases (e.g., a cluster of shootings), closing a case includes preparing a simple narrative that can be shared at a neighborhood meeting: what happened, how it was addressed, and what prevention steps are in place.

items.title: Detectives as named liaisons to key institutions
items.desc: Specific detectives are assigned as regular contact points for school systems, hospitals, major housing providers, and youth agencies. Their work includes quarterly information-sharing meetings and joint problem-solving with these partners, not just subpoena or service-of-process interactions.

items.title: SWAT / tactical front-end planning with community input
items.desc: For planned operations (search warrants, high-risk arrests), a short community impact review is required before execution: who lives nearby, recent community complaints, known vulnerable residents, and a post-operation plan for explaining what happened. After action, a supervisor makes at least one proactive, non-enforcement contact with key stakeholders such as a neighborhood association, pastor, or property manager.

items.title: Gang and violence units co-designing interventions
items.desc: When targeting hotspots or specific groups, these units spend part of their week in formal call-ins or small meetings with community leaders, outreach workers, and at-risk individuals, pairing enforcement messages with connections to services.

items.title: Traffic unit operating as a neighborhood safety team
items.desc: Traffic officers adopt specific corridors and hold quarterly walk-throughs with residents and business owners to identify environmental fixes (crosswalks, lighting, signage), then coordinate with public works to act on them. Performance includes tracking reductions in community-reported near-misses, not just crashes and citations.

items.title: Visible positive presence between operations
items.desc: Between high-risk operations, tactical and specialized crime units schedule non-enforcement presence at youth sports, community events, or "Coffee with a Cop"-style gatherings in their assigned areas. Attendance is built into their duty schedule a few times per month, not treated as a voluntary add-on.

items.title: Community impact section in all operation debriefs
items.desc: Every operation debrief includes a structured section on community impact and "problem roots": what recurring issue prompted the need for this operation, and what upstream, community-based strategies could reduce similar future operations.

items.title: Performance evaluations tied to community outcomes
items.desc: Annual evaluations include explicit, scored categories: "Problem solving," "Community partnerships," and "Responsiveness to residents," with concrete examples required from each officer's SARA projects and community contact logs.

items.title: Promotion criteria that reflect community policing
items.desc: Leadership of at least one documented, successful problem-solving initiative, plus positive feedback from community partners, is a formal prerequisite for promotion to sergeant and above.

items.title: Problem-focused command reviews, not just crime counts
items.desc: Regular command meetings (CompStat-style) focus on which recurring problems were identified, what partnerships were activated, and what changed in conditions, not only on arrest numbers and clearance rates.

items.title: FTO program includes community policing competencies
items.desc: Field training officers are required to demonstrate and actively coach community contact skills, problem-solving methods, and relationship mapping. These are evaluated as core competencies alongside tactics and report writing, not treated as soft extras.

references.title: COPS Office "Community Policing Defined" model
references.desc: The DOJ's COPS Office defines community policing as a tripod of organizational transformation, community partnerships, and problem-solving using the SARA model. Provides a ready-made framework for requiring every unit to document partnerships and problem-solving as part of normal work. Source: cops.usdoj.gov

references.title: 21st Century Policing Task Force cities
references.desc: Cities including Birmingham, Stockton, and Gary increased officer participation in community forums, neighborhood clean-ups, youth sports, and anti-crime strategies with civic partners, during duty hours, not as overtime. Source: obamawhitehouse.archives.gov

references.title: "Coffee with a Cop" (originated Hawthorne, CA)
references.desc: Informal coffee events at everyday venues so officers and residents can talk without the pressure of calls for service. Easy to embed in regular patrol schedules and to rotate detectives and specialized units through on a set schedule. Now active in departments across the U.S. Source: surfcitync.gov

references.title: Neighborhood-based beats and foot/bike patrols
references.desc: Widely adopted across U.S. agencies: officers assigned to small geographic areas for extended periods, with face-to-face interactions prioritized. The structural lever is redesigning patrol deployment so "owning a beat" and knowing stakeholders is formally evaluated, not optional. Source: OJP, policing literature

references.title: Youth engagement and school-based initiatives (SROs + community programming)
references.desc: Officers partner with schools to run mentoring, safety education, and problem-solving around disorder and violence near campuses. Detectives and patrol can be assigned as regular school liaisons as part of their caseload or beat responsibilities. Source: amu.apus.edu

references.title: Problem-oriented policing using SARA (DOJ/OJP)
references.desc: Officers identify recurring problems, analyze underlying causes, implement tailored responses with partners, and assess results. OJP documentation gives a template for requiring each squad or unit to run at least one SARA project per year as part of standard duties and evaluation. Source: ojp.gov

references.title: Inter-American Development Bank: multi-country community policing evidence
references.desc: Documented in Brazil, Colombia, the Philippines, Liberia, Pakistan, and Uganda. Common elements: increased foot patrols, regular community meetings, and collaborative problem-solving on citizen-identified concerns. When implementation leads to responsive action by police, interventions tend to build trust and cooperation. Source: plataformadeevidencias.iadb.org

references.title: UCLA study: what makes community policing fail
references.desc: Rigorous evaluations across six countries found that add-on meetings and short pilots, without real changes to how officers are supervised and evaluated, rarely move outcomes. The core lesson: community policing must be embedded as a standard operating philosophy (beats, partnerships, problem-solving, accountability), not a time-limited project. Source: UCLA Luskin / newsroom.ucla.edu

references.title: United Nations Police: community-oriented policing in peace operations
references.desc: UN policing guidelines stress that community policing must be an overall approach for the entire police service, not just for specialized "community liaison" officers. Emphasizes building public trust, forming partnerships, and reforming host-state police agencies around these principles. Source: police.un.org
